Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

It sells pantry staples, cleaning supplies, seeds, and a rotating selection of local produce. The shop has one checkout counter and a folding table near the entrance where volunteers sort deliveries. Members take turns staffing the counter, while a paid coordinator handles the weekly supplier orders. The shop has used a shared spreadsheet for several years, but a volunteer is trying a short Python utility for some internal calculations. The request is about the supplied function, not a request to design a new checkout system.

Prices on the shelves are displayed in dollars, and the shop’s printed receipts show dollar amounts with two digits after the decimal point. Some items are sold by the piece, while others are weighed and priced from a label prepared by the produce scale. On busy Saturdays, checkout volunteers sometimes jot down prices on a paper tally before entering them into the register. The tally may contain prices from different departments, but the supplied function receives a list called `prices`; the notes do not say how that list is assembled or what kinds of values it can contain.

The coordinator, Mara Venn, said that the utility came up during a conversation about a monthly member-credit report. “I only want to know what this little function does with the values it gets,” she said. A volunteer named Ivo Park asked whether a compact example could help new cashiers understand it, but no example input or expected output is included here. Neither Mara nor Ivo described a formal accounting policy, and they did not say that the function is currently used to charge customers or issue credits.

The shop’s context has changed a little over the last year. Cedar Loop started carrying jars of honey from a nearby apiary, and those jars are priced individually rather than by weight. The seed shelf also has a few low-cost packets whose displayed price is less than one dollar. The coordinator keeps a separate ledger for donated goods, so not every product mentioned in a volunteer’s handwritten tally necessarily represents a customer sale. These details explain the setting, but the notes do not establish that any of these products or ledger entries are passed to the function.

1. At the first planning meeting each month, the volunteers review a draft member-credit sheet beside the counter. Mara checks the supplier invoices, while Ivo compares several lines with the spreadsheet. Another volunteer, Noor, writes down questions on a blue index card so the group can discuss them after the shop closes. Their process is informal; the notes do not specify a required formula for member credits or a particular rounding policy. The function below was shared in that discussion, and the group wanted a plain-language account of its behavior before considering whether it was relevant to the spreadsheet.

2. The volunteers sometimes talk about totals in cents because the register export has a cents column, even though shelf labels use dollars. A volunteer recalled that “the odd little forty-two at the end caught my eye,” but did not explain why it is present. Ivo wondered aloud whether it was a temporary adjustment or simply a value added by the person who wrote the function. That question is unresolved in the notes. The code itself is the only supplied evidence about how the function computes its return value, so a review should distinguish what can be read directly from the code from guesses about the reason for any particular operation.

There is also a conditional detail from a discussion about future spreadsheet imports: if the shop later feeds the function values taken from receipt lines, those values may already have been rounded for display; if instead it feeds unrounded values from a scale calculation, the values could have a different precision. The volunteers have not said which of those situations applies to the list passed here. No input examples, test results, or surrounding program are supplied, and the notes do not establish that either kind of value is actually passed to this function today.

During the last inventory afternoon, Noor set aside a basket of bruised pears for the community-fridge table and marked its paper tally separately from the sale items. Ivo asked whether a price total could be used to reconcile the basket with the register, and Mara replied, “That depends on what we put into the list first.” The exchange did not settle how donated items should be represented in software. It does show why the group wants the function’s behavior described without treating every shop tally as interchangeable with a customer’s bill. The volunteers also use a small calculator at the counter, but no details about its settings or behavior are available.

The shop is preparing a short handout for its next volunteer orientation, when two new members will learn how the spreadsheet and register exports are discussed at closing time. The handout is not drafted, and nobody has chosen a policy change or approved a software update. The group’s immediate question is limited to the supplied code: what it does with the `prices` argument, what a reviewer can responsibly notice from the code alone, and what small tests would make its behavior easier to check. If the available context leaves a point undecided, the explanation should leave it undecided too.

def total_cents(prices):
    total = 0
    for price in prices:
        total += round(price * 100)
